sections.h2: Who inherits a New York house with no will?
sections.html:
Under Estates, Powers and Trusts Law section 4-1.1, inheritance runs from the spouse and children outward through parents, siblings, grandparents and more distant relatives. Each share is figured after debts, administration expenses and reasonable funeral costs are subtracted.

Intestate distribution in New York
SurvivorsWho takes the estate
Spouse and children or other issue$50,000 and half of the rest to the spouse, the balance to the issue
Spouse, no issueAll to the spouse
Issue, no spouseAll to the issue, by representation
Parents onlyAll to the surviving parent or parents
Issue of parents onlyAll to those siblings and their issue
Grandparents or their issue onlySplit by paternal and maternal side

Half-blood relatives are treated as whole-blood relatives. A child conceived before the death and born alive afterward inherits as if born during the decedent's life. The spouse's share is in place of any right of dower.

A small estate is one where the decedent left personal property with a gross value of $50,000 or less, not counting property set off for the family under EPTL 5-3.1(a). Surrogate's Court Procedure Act section 1301 defines it that way, and such an estate can be settled by a voluntary administrator without formal court administration.

The definition counts personal property, and a house is real property. Before you rely on the voluntary route for an estate that includes real estate, call the Surrogate's Court clerk in the decedent's county. The $50,000 figure alone doesn't decide it.

Where the route is available, section 1304 keeps it light:

  • There is no waiting period after the death.
  • The voluntary administrator posts no bond.
  • The applicant files an affidavit and a certified copy of the death certificate with the clerk of the court in the county where the decedent lived.
  • No court order or hearing is needed, and a short certificate from the court shows the person's authority to banks and others holding the decedent's property.

sections.h2: Who can be a voluntary administrator?
sections.html:
With no will, the right goes first to the surviving adult spouse. If there is none, or the spouse renounces, it passes in order to an adult child or grandchild, parent, sibling, niece or nephew, or aunt or uncle. Section 1303 then moves to a guardian or committee for a distributee who can't act, and finally to the chief fiscal officer of the county in counties without a public administrator.

If there is a will, the named executor or alternate executor has the first right and acts by filing the will with the surrogate's court. When that person renounces or fails to qualify by filing the required affidavit within thirty days after the will is filed, an adult who could petition for letters of administration with will annexed may step in. Nobody outside those lists can serve.

sections.h2: Letters of administration when there is no will
sections.html:
The court follows the priority list in section 1001, and letters go to eligible, qualified distributees in this order:

  • the surviving spouse;
  • the children;
  • the grandchildren;
  • either parent;
  • the brothers or sisters;
  • any other distributee, with preference to the one entitled to the largest share.

Equally entitled distributees can share the appointment. The court can also grant letters to a non-distributee, or to a trust company, when all eligible distributees file acknowledged consents. When no eligible person accepts, letters go to the public administrator or the county's chief fiscal officer, then to the petitioner at the court's discretion.

If relatives disagree about who should serve, talk to a New York probate attorney before filing. Ask the attorney who holds authority to sign a deed before any listing goes up.

The court issues letters of administration with the will annexed, using the priority in section 1418. A sole beneficiary comes first, then one or more residuary beneficiaries, then other people interested in the estate.

If no eligible person will accept, letters issue to the public administrator or, where there is none, the county treasurer. The court may then turn to the petitioner or someone it designates. Beneficiaries can also consent to the appointment of a person who isn't a beneficiary, or of a trust company, if all eligible beneficiaries sign acknowledged consents.

sections.h2: Can an executor sell the house before probate is finished?
sections.html:
Sometimes. Under section 1412, a named executor can ask for preliminary letters once a probate petition is filed and process has issued. Those letters carry an administrator's powers, with one limit: they don't allow paying a legacy or distributive share.

Unless the court or the will says otherwise, a preliminary executor may take possession of, manage and sell real property devised by the will. If the house is specifically devised to someone, it can be sold only with that devisee's written consent or by court order. The preliminary executor must give notice of the appointment to all parties who have appeared within ten days.

The court may limit the letters to certain assets, and may revoke them for unreasonable delay in the probate proceeding.

sections.h2: What a fiduciary can do with a house
sections.html:
Absent contrary terms in the will or the court order, EPTL section 11-1.1 gives a fiduciary broad powers over estate property. For a house, the most relevant are:

  • to take possession, collect rents and manage it;
  • to sell it at public or private sale, on terms the fiduciary believes most advantageous to the people interested, unless the property is specifically disposed of;
  • to lease it for up to three years, or up to ten for a trustee;
  • to grant an option to buy for up to six months;
  • to insure it and make ordinary repairs;
  • to sign deeds, contracts and other documents needed to administer the estate.

A power the will forbids can still be exercised with the surrogate's approval when needed for the purposes in SCPA 1902. The court may also authorize powers the statute doesn't list.

sections.h2: Transfer tax on an inherited house
sections.html:
Passing a house to an heir triggers no transfer tax, because a conveyance doesn't include a transfer by devise, bequest or inheritance. A later sale by the estate or an heir is a conveyance like any other, with the base tax of $2 per $500 paid by the seller.

If that sale reaches $1 million or more, the buyer owes the additional mansion tax, and the seller becomes liable if the buyer doesn't pay. Ask the closing attorney to prepare the transfer tax return before the date of delivery, since it is due by the fifteenth day after the deed is delivered. The state transfer tax page has the forms.

faqs.q: How much does a spouse inherit in New York without a will?
faqs.a: It depends on who else survives. With children, the spouse takes $50,000 plus half of the remainder. With no children or other issue, the spouse takes everything. The calculation starts after debts, administration costs and reasonable funeral expenses are taken out.

faqs.q: Does a New York small estate include real estate?
faqs.a: The statutory definition looks at personal property of $50,000 or less and doesn't mention a house. Ask the Surrogate's Court clerk in the county where the decedent lived whether voluntary administration can reach your situation before relying on it.

faqs.q: Who can sign the deed on an inherited New York house?
faqs.a: The power to sell belongs to the fiduciary the court appoints, such as an executor or administrator. Preliminary letters can also carry that power when a probate petition is pending, with consent rules if the house was specifically devised.

faqs.q: Do I need a bond to administer a small estate in New York?
faqs.a: No, a voluntary administrator doesn't need to give a bond. The person files an affidavit and a certified death certificate with the clerk of the court in the decedent's county. A short certificate from the court then proves the authority to act.

faqs.q: What happens if no family member will serve as administrator?
faqs.a: Letters can issue to the public administrator or, in counties without one, to the chief fiscal officer of the county. The court may also appoint the petitioner or another person it designates. Consents from all eligible distributees can allow a trust company or a non-relative to serve.
